concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Typical and atypical thoracic vertebrae
concepts.summary: This concept integrates typical and atypical thoracic vertebrae across the cited cardiovascular sources. Typical T2-T8 vertebrae have superior and inferior costal demifacets on the body and a transverse costal facet for the rib tubercle. T1 has a complete superior facet for rib 1 and an inferior demifacet; T10-T12 progressively lose the typical paired-facet pattern.
keyPoints: Typical T2-T8 vertebrae have superior and inferior costal demifacets on the body and a transverse costal facet for the rib tubercle.
T1 has a complete superior facet for rib 1 and an inferior demifacet; T10-T12 progressively lose the typical paired-facet pattern.
T11 and T12 lack transverse costal facets because ribs 11 and 12 have no costotransverse joints.
Long inferiorly directed spinous processes and overlapping laminae characterize the mid-thoracic region and constrain extension.
examTraps: Do not call every thoracic vertebra typical: T1, T9, T10, T11, and T12 have distinct costal-facet patterns.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of typical and atypical thoracic vertebrae.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Typical T2-T8 vertebrae have superior and inferior costal demifacets on the body and a transverse costal facet for the rib tubercle. T1 has a complete superior facet for rib 1 and an inferior demifacet; T10-T12 progressively lose the typical paired-facet pattern.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Typical and atypical ribs
concepts.summary: This concept integrates typical and atypical ribs across the cited cardiovascular sources. A typical rib has a head with two articular facets, a neck, tubercle, angle, shaft, and an inferior internal costal groove. The first rib is broad and flat with scalene tubercle and grooves for the subclavian vein anteriorly and artery posteriorly.
keyPoints: A typical rib has a head with two articular facets, a neck, tubercle, angle, shaft, and an inferior internal costal groove.
The first rib is broad and flat with scalene tubercle and grooves for the subclavian vein anteriorly and artery posteriorly.
Rib 2 has a tuberosity for serratus anterior, whereas ribs 10-12 have single head facets and ribs 11-12 lack necks and tubercles.
Costal cartilages prolong ribs anteriorly; ribs 1-7 attach directly, 8-10 join the cartilage above, and 11-12 are floating.
examTraps: The subclavian vein lies anterior to the scalene tubercle; the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus lie posterior.
The costal groove is on the inferior internal border, but the collateral bundle runs near the superior border of the rib below.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of typical and atypical ribs.
retrievalPrompts.answer: A typical rib has a head with two articular facets, a neck, tubercle, angle, shaft, and an inferior internal costal groove. The first rib is broad and flat with scalene tubercle and grooves for the subclavian vein anteriorly and artery posteriorly.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Sternum and palpable landmarks
concepts.summary: This concept integrates sternum and palpable landmarks across the cited cardiovascular sources. The sternum comprises manubrium, body, and xiphoid process, with the jugular notch at the superior manubrium. The manubriosternal joint forms the sternal angle at the level of the second costal cartilage and the T4-T5 intervertebral disc.
keyPoints: The sternum comprises manubrium, body, and xiphoid process, with the jugular notch at the superior manubrium.
The manubriosternal joint forms the sternal angle at the level of the second costal cartilage and the T4-T5 intervertebral disc.
The sternal angle is the landmark for rib counting, tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch, and the transverse thoracic plane.
The xiphisternal joint is near T9 and marks the inferior limit of the central thoracic cavity and the infrasternal angle.
examTraps: The first rib is difficult to palpate; identify the second costal cartilage at the sternal angle before counting ribs.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of sternum and palpable landmarks.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The sternum comprises manubrium, body, and xiphoid process, with the jugular notch at the superior manubrium. The manubriosternal joint forms the sternal angle at the level of the second costal cartilage and the T4-T5 intervertebral disc.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Thoracic apertures and cavity boundaries
concepts.summary: This concept integrates thoracic apertures and cavity boundaries across the cited cardiovascular sources. The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by T1, the first ribs and their cartilages, and the superior manubrial border. The oblique first-rib plane makes the aperture higher posteriorly than anteriorly and permits passage of trachea, esophagus, great vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
keyPoints: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by T1, the first ribs and their cartilages, and the superior manubrial border.
The oblique first-rib plane makes the aperture higher posteriorly than anteriorly and permits passage of trachea, esophagus, great vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
The inferior aperture is bounded by T12, ribs 11-12, the costal margin, and xiphisternal joint and is closed by the diaphragm.
The thoracic wall encloses pleural cavities laterally and the mediastinum centrally, while communicating superiorly with the neck.
examTraps: The inferior thoracic aperture is an osteocartilaginous boundary, not an open hole in life; the diaphragm closes it.

retrievalPrompts.answer: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by T1, the first ribs and their cartilages, and the superior manubrial border. The oblique first-rib plane makes the aperture higher posteriorly than anteriorly and permits passage of trachea, esophagus, great vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Vertebral joints, ligaments, and intervertebral discs
concepts.summary: This concept integrates vertebral joints, ligaments, and intervertebral discs across the cited cardiovascular sources. Vertebral bodies are united by secondary cartilaginous intervertebral joints, while articular processes form plane synovial facet joints. Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments limit extension and flexion respectively; ligamenta flava join adjacent laminae.
keyPoints: Vertebral bodies are united by secondary cartilaginous intervertebral joints, while articular processes form plane synovial facet joints.
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments limit extension and flexion respectively; ligamenta flava join adjacent laminae.
An intervertebral disc has an outer annulus fibrosus surrounding a hydrated nucleus pulposus that distributes compression.
Posterolateral annular failure can permit nucleus pulposus herniation toward a spinal nerve root because the posterior longitudinal ligament is relatively narrow laterally.
examTraps: A disc lesion is named for the disc level, but the affected traversing nerve root may have the number of the vertebra below in lumbar examples.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of vertebral joints, ligaments, and intervertebral discs.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vertebral bodies are united by secondary cartilaginous intervertebral joints, while articular processes form plane synovial facet joints. Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments limit extension and flexion respectively; ligamenta flava join adjacent laminae.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Costovertebral, costotransverse, and anterior costal joints
concepts.summary: This concept integrates costovertebral, costotransverse, and anterior costal joints across the cited cardiovascular sources. A typical rib head articulates with its numerically corresponding vertebra, the vertebra above, and the intervening disc. The rib tubercle forms a synovial costotransverse joint with the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra.
keyPoints: A typical rib head articulates with its numerically corresponding vertebra, the vertebra above, and the intervening disc.
The rib tubercle forms a synovial costotransverse joint with the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra.
The first sternocostal joint is primary cartilaginous; sternocostal joints 2-7 are generally synovial.
Costochondral joints are primary cartilaginous, whereas interchondral joints between lower costal cartilages are usually synovial.
examTraps: Ribs 11 and 12 do not form costotransverse joints because they lack tubercles and T11-T12 lack transverse costal facets.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of costovertebral, costotransverse, and anterior costal joints.
retrievalPrompts.answer: A typical rib head articulates with its numerically corresponding vertebra, the vertebra above, and the intervening disc. The rib tubercle forms a synovial costotransverse joint with the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pump-handle and bucket-handle mechanics
concepts.summary: This concept integrates pump-handle and bucket-handle mechanics across the cited cardiovascular sources. Upper ribs rotate to move the sternum anteriorly and superiorly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter in a pump-handle motion. Lower ribs elevate laterally, increasing the transverse diameter in a bucket-handle motion.
keyPoints: Upper ribs rotate to move the sternum anteriorly and superiorly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter in a pump-handle motion.
Lower ribs elevate laterally, increasing the transverse diameter in a bucket-handle motion.
Costovertebral and costotransverse joint geometry determines the axis about which each rib moves.
Diaphragmatic descent increases the vertical diameter and acts with rib elevation during inspiration.
examTraps: Pump-handle and bucket-handle movements describe different predominant thoracic diameters; they are not interchangeable labels for all ribs.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Upper ribs rotate to move the sternum anteriorly and superiorly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter in a pump-handle motion. Lower ribs elevate laterally, increasing the transverse diameter in a bucket-handle motion.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Thoracic cage and vertebral clinical variants
concepts.summary: This concept integrates thoracic cage and vertebral clinical variants across the cited cardiovascular sources. Pectus excavatum depresses the sternum, whereas pectus carinatum produces anterior protrusion of the chest wall. A cervical rib from C7 can compress the lower brachial plexus or subclavian vessels at the thoracic outlet.
keyPoints: Pectus excavatum depresses the sternum, whereas pectus carinatum produces anterior protrusion of the chest wall.
A cervical rib from C7 can compress the lower brachial plexus or subclavian vessels at the thoracic outlet.
Hemivertebra can produce congenital scoliosis; osteoporosis and vertebral metastases predispose to compression fracture.
Spina bifida reflects failure of vertebral arch fusion, while spondylolisthesis denotes anterior vertebral displacement.
examTraps: Cervical-rib neurologic symptoms usually involve the lower trunk (C8-T1), not the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of thoracic cage and vertebral clinical variants.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Pectus excavatum depresses the sternum, whereas pectus carinatum produces anterior protrusion of the chest wall. A cervical rib from C7 can compress the lower brachial plexus or subclavian vessels at the thoracic outlet.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Intercostal muscle layers
concepts.summary: This concept integrates intercostal muscle layers across the cited cardiovascular sources. External intercostals run inferoanteriorly and are replaced anteriorly by external intercostal membranes. Internal intercostals run inferoposteriorly and are replaced posteriorly by internal intercostal membranes.
keyPoints: External intercostals run inferoanteriorly and are replaced anteriorly by external intercostal membranes.
Internal intercostals run inferoposteriorly and are replaced posteriorly by internal intercostal membranes.
Innermost intercostals share the internal layer's fiber direction but are separated from it by the intercostal neurovascular plane.
External intercostals assist inspiration; interosseous internal intercostals aid forced expiration, while interchondral internal fibers can elevate ribs.
examTraps: The neurovascular bundle does not lie between external and internal intercostals; it lies between internal and innermost layers.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of intercostal muscle layers.
retrievalPrompts.answer: External intercostals run inferoanteriorly and are replaced anteriorly by external intercostal membranes. Internal intercostals run inferoposteriorly and are replaced posteriorly by internal intercostal membranes.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Transversus thoracis, subcostales, and levatores costarum
concepts.summary: This concept integrates transversus thoracis, subcostales, and levatores costarum across the cited cardiovascular sources. Transversus thoracis spans from the posterior sternum to internal surfaces of costal cartilages and weakly depresses ribs. Subcostales are best developed posteriorly, span more than one rib, and share the internal intercostal fiber direction.
keyPoints: Transversus thoracis spans from the posterior sternum to internal surfaces of costal cartilages and weakly depresses ribs.
Subcostales are best developed posteriorly, span more than one rib, and share the internal intercostal fiber direction.
Levatores costarum arise from transverse processes and elevate ribs, assisting inspiration and lateral flexion.
These discontinuous muscles complete the innermost muscular layer at anterior, lateral, and posterior parts of the thoracic wall.
examTraps: Transversus thoracis is on the internal anterior wall and is closely related to the internal thoracic vessels; do not confuse it with transversus abdominis.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Transversus thoracis spans from the posterior sternum to internal surfaces of costal cartilages and weakly depresses ribs. Subcostales are best developed posteriorly, span more than one rib, and share the internal intercostal fiber direction.

concepts.title: Pectoral muscles and serratus anterior
concepts.summary: This concept integrates pectoral muscles and serratus anterior across the cited cardiovascular sources. Pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the humerus; its clavicular head flexes and sternocostal fibers extend a flexed arm. Pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3-5 to the coracoid and stabilizes the scapula by drawing it anteriorly and inferiorly.
keyPoints: Pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the humerus; its clavicular head flexes and sternocostal fibers extend a flexed arm.
Pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3-5 to the coracoid and stabilizes the scapula by drawing it anteriorly and inferiorly.
Subclavius anchors the clavicle to rib 1 and helps protect the underlying subclavian vessels and brachial plexus.
Serratus anterior protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula; long thoracic nerve injury causes medial scapular winging.
examTraps: Scapular winging after axillary surgery implicates the long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior, not the medial or lateral pectoral nerves.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Diaphragm attachments, openings, and innervation
concepts.summary: This concept integrates diaphragm attachments, openings, and innervation across the cited cardiovascular sources. The diaphragm arises from xiphoid, lower six costal elements, and lumbar crura/arcuate ligaments and inserts into a central tendon. The caval opening at T8 transmits the inferior vena cava; the esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits esophagus and vagal trunks; the aortic hiatus at T12 transmits aorta and thoracic duct.

The caval opening at T8 transmits the inferior vena cava; the esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits esophagus and vagal trunks; the aortic hiatus at T12 transmits aorta and thoracic duct.
Phrenic nerves provide motor supply and central sensory innervation; peripheral sensory fibers travel with lower intercostal nerves.
Contraction descends the domes to enlarge thoracic volume, while the right dome normally lies higher because of the liver.
examTraps: The aorta passes behind the diaphragm through the aortic hiatus, so diaphragmatic contraction does not constrict it like the esophageal hiatus.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Breast fascia, blood supply, and lymphatic drainage
concepts.summary: This concept integrates breast fascia, blood supply, and lymphatic drainage across the cited cardiovascular sources. The breast lies in superficial fascia, mainly over pectoralis major, and extends toward the axilla as the axillary tail. Suspensory ligaments connect dermis to deep fascia; malignant shortening can produce skin dimpling.
keyPoints: The breast lies in superficial fascia, mainly over pectoralis major, and extends toward the axilla as the axillary tail.
Suspensory ligaments connect dermis to deep fascia; malignant shortening can produce skin dimpling.
Blood arrives from perforating internal thoracic branches, lateral thoracic artery, and posterior intercostal branches.
Most lymph drains to axillary nodes, especially the pectoral group; medial drainage can cross to parasternal nodes and the opposite breast.
examTraps: The retromammary space permits breast mobility over pectoral fascia; fixation suggests invasion rather than normal ligament anatomy.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Internal thoracic and anterior intercostal arteries
concepts.summary: This concept integrates internal thoracic and anterior intercostal arteries across the cited cardiovascular sources. The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian and descends just lateral to the sternum behind upper costal cartilages. It supplies paired anterior intercostal arteries to the upper six spaces and terminates near the sixth space as musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.
keyPoints: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian and descends just lateral to the sternum behind upper costal cartilages.
It supplies paired anterior intercostal arteries to the upper six spaces and terminates near the sixth space as musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.
Pericardiacophrenic branches accompany phrenic nerves and supply pericardium, pleura, and diaphragm.
Perforating, sternal, thymic, mediastinal, and pericardial branches create important thoracic-wall and breast anastomoses.
examTraps: Lower anterior intercostal arteries arise from the musculophrenic continuation, not directly from the thoracic aorta.

retrievalPrompts.answer: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian and descends just lateral to the sternum behind upper costal cartilages. It supplies paired anterior intercostal arteries to the upper six spaces and terminates near the sixth space as musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.

Proximal sixth arches form proximal pulmonary arteries, while distal left sixth persists as ductus arteriosus and distal right regresses.
Recurrent laryngeal nerves are trapped by persisting vessels: right under subclavian artery and left under aortic arch/ductus arteriosus.
examTraps: The arch of aorta is not derived solely from left fourth arch; aortic sac and left dorsal aorta also contribute adjacent segments.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of pharyngeal arch artery derivatives and recurrent nerves.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Third arches form common carotids and proximal internal carotids. Left fourth contributes aortic arch; right fourth contributes proximal right subclavian artery.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Dorsal aortae, vitelline/umbilical arteries, and major arterial derivatives
concepts.summary: The dorsal aortae and their branches remodel into definitive arteries. In the cited local 15th-edition Langman passage, persisting vitelline arteries are represented by the celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery, whereas the inferior mesenteric artery is attributed there to the umbilical-artery system; this catalog follows that source-specific convention rather than asserting a universal three-vessel vitelline list.
keyPoints: The paired dorsal aortae fuse caudally and selectively regress or persist as definitive arterial segments.
In the cited local Langman 15e text, the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries represent persisting vitelline arteries.
That same local passage attributes the inferior mesenteric artery to the umbilical-artery system; terminology differs among teaching sources, so answer to the cited course/book convention.
After birth, proximal umbilical arteries remain as superior vesical arteries, while distal portions become medial umbilical ligaments.
examTraps: Do not expand the local source claim to all three unpaired gut arteries: the cited local Langman passage explicitly names celiac and superior mesenteric as vitelline and places inferior mesenteric with the umbilical system.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: According to the cited local Langman passage, which adult arteries represent persisting vitelline arteries?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery; the same local passage assigns the inferior mesenteric artery to the umbilical-artery system.

objectives.text: Explain and apply the defining relationships of dorsal aortae, vitelline/umbilical arteries, and major arterial derivatives.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Vitelline, umbilical, and cardinal venous remodeling
concepts.summary: This concept integrates vitelline, umbilical, and cardinal venous remodeling across the cited cardiovascular sources. Vitelline veins form hepatic sinusoids, portal vein, and a major hepatic segment of IVC. Right umbilical vein regresses; left umbilical vein carries placental blood and later becomes ligamentum teres hepatis.
keyPoints: Vitelline veins form hepatic sinusoids, portal vein, and a major hepatic segment of IVC.
Right umbilical vein regresses; left umbilical vein carries placental blood and later becomes ligamentum teres hepatis.
Anterior cardinal veins and their anastomosis contribute brachiocephalic veins and SVC, with right common cardinal vein contributing SVC.
Subcardinal, supracardinal, and posterior cardinal systems remodel into renal, gonadal, azygos, iliac, and IVC segments.
examTraps: The IVC has multiple embryonic segments; assigning the entire vessel to a single cardinal vein is incorrect.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of vitelline, umbilical, and cardinal venous remodeling.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vitelline veins form hepatic sinusoids, portal vein, and a major hepatic segment of IVC. Right umbilical vein regresses; left umbilical vein carries placental blood and later becomes ligamentum teres hepatis.

objectives.text: Explain and apply the defining relationships of vitelline, umbilical, and cardinal venous remodeling.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Fetal circulation and transition at birth
concepts.summary: This concept integrates fetal circulation and transition at birth across the cited cardiovascular sources. Oxygenated placental blood travels through left umbilical vein and mostly bypasses liver through ductus venosus to IVC. Preferential streaming across foramen ovale supplies left heart, while right-ventricular output largely reaches descending aorta through ductus arteriosus.
keyPoints: Oxygenated placental blood travels through left umbilical vein and mostly bypasses liver through ductus venosus to IVC.
Preferential streaming across foramen ovale supplies left heart, while right-ventricular output largely reaches descending aorta through ductus arteriosus.
First breaths lower pulmonary resistance and cord clamping raises systemic resistance, increasing left relative to right atrial pressure.
Functional closure of foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus, and umbilical vessels precedes later anatomical remodeling into adult ligaments.
examTraps: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood toward fetus, whereas umbilical arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood toward placenta.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of fetal circulation and transition at birth.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Oxygenated placental blood travels through left umbilical vein and mostly bypasses liver through ductus venosus to IVC. Preferential streaming across foramen ovale supplies left heart, while right-ventricular output largely reaches descending aorta through ductus arteriosus.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Lymph-sac and lymphatic-vessel development
concepts.summary: This concept integrates lymph-sac and lymphatic-vessel development across the cited cardiovascular sources. Lymphatic endothelial channels arise in close association with embryonic venous endothelium and coalesce into primary lymph sacs. Paired jugular, iliac, retroperitoneal, and cisterna chyli regions contribute to the developing network.
keyPoints: Lymphatic endothelial channels arise in close association with embryonic venous endothelium and coalesce into primary lymph sacs.
Paired jugular, iliac, retroperitoneal, and cisterna chyli regions contribute to the developing network.
Longitudinal channels and anastomoses form thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct with selective regression.
Lymph nodes develop as mesenchyme invades lymph sacs and reorganizes channels, whereas spleen develops separately in dorsal mesogastric mesenchyme.
examTraps: Spleen is a lymphoid organ but does not develop from a lymph sac; it arises in mesenchyme of the dorsal mesogastrium.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the examinable core of lymph-sac and lymphatic-vessel development.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lymphatic endothelial channels arise in close association with embryonic venous endothelium and coalesce into primary lymph sacs. Paired jugular, iliac, retroperitoneal, and cisterna chyli regions contribute to the developing network.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Endocardium, valves, cardiac skeleton, and conducting tissue
concepts.summary: The endocardium is a chamber-facing endothelial sheet supported by fibroelastic connective tissue and a deeper subendocardial compartment that merges with myocardium. That deeper compartment carries vessels, nerves, and conducting fibers. Valve cusps are collagen-rich extensions of the fibrous skeleton covered by nonthrombogenic endothelium. The cardiac skeleton supports valve attachments and electrically insulates atria from ventricles so that normal activation is channeled through the atrioventricular conducting system. Purkinje fibers are large, pale, glycogen-rich modified myocytes with sparse peripheral myofibrils in the ventricular subendocardium.
keyPoints: Endocardium progresses from endothelium to fibroelastic support and then a subendocardial layer continuous with myocardium.
Valve cusps are connective-tissue cores covered on both sides by endothelium; an incomplete endothelial surface is thrombogenic.
The fibrous cardiac skeleton is both mechanical support and atrioventricular electrical insulation.
SA nodal cells are smaller and less myofibril-rich than working atrial cells; Purkinje fibers are larger, pale, glycogen-rich subendocardial cells.
examTraps: Do not place Purkinje fibers in the epicardium or confuse their pale glycogen-rich cytoplasm with adipocytes.
Do not call the blood-contacting valve surface mesothelium; it is endothelium.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why are Purkinje fibers pale and where are they found?
retrievalPrompts.answer: They contain abundant glycogen and relatively few peripheral myofibrils and lie in the ventricular subendocardial conducting network.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does the cardiac skeleton shape electrical activation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its dense connective tissue insulates atrial from ventricular myocardium, restricting normal atrioventricular conduction to the specialized bundle.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Cardiac-muscle ultrastructure, coupling, endocrine role, and repair
concepts.summary: Cardiac myocytes are branching striated cells with central nuclei, abundant mitochondria, and end-to-end intercalated discs. Transverse disc regions contain fascia adherens and desmosomes for force transmission, whereas longitudinal regions are rich in gap junctions for electrical continuity. Cardiac excitation-contraction junctions are dyads—one T tubule and one terminal cistern—usually near Z discs; ventricular T tubules are more developed than atrial ones. Atrial granules contain atrial natriuretic factor precursor. Adult myocardium lacks a useful satellite-cell pool, so infarct repair is dominated by scar.
keyPoints: Fascia adherens and desmosomes provide mechanical linkage; gap junctions provide electrical coupling.
Cardiac dyads differ from skeletal triads in both composition and position.
Atrial secretory granules support an endocrine natriuretic/diuretic function.
Adult cardiac muscle has very limited regenerative capacity and lacks skeletal-muscle-like satellite cells.
examTraps: Preserved gap junctions do not rescue a defect in disc adhesion.
Atrial contractile cells may have tiny or absent T tubules; that does not make them conduction cells.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is a cardiac dyad?
retrievalPrompts.answer: One T tubule apposed to one terminal cistern, generally near a Z disc.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which intercalated-disc components carry force and which carry current?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Fascia adherens and desmosomes transmit force; gap junctions permit ionic current between cells.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Endothelium and integrated vascular-wall biology
concepts.summary: Endothelium is an active selective interface, not inert lining. It governs transcytosis, barrier permeability, hemostatic and fibrinolytic balance, leukocyte recruitment, vascular tone, and angiogenesis. Weibel-Palade bodies store rapidly deployable P-selectin and von Willebrand factor. Nitric oxide and prostacyclin oppose endothelin-driven contraction. VEGF drives endothelial sprouting, while angiopoietin signaling recruits mural cells and fibroblasts. In large vessels, luminal diffusion feeds the intima and vasa vasorum feed adventitia and outer media; nervi vasorum act chiefly on medial smooth muscle.
keyPoints: Endothelial transport includes diffusion, receptor-mediated uptake, and transcytosis.
P-selectin deployment from Weibel-Palade bodies initiates leukocyte rolling before integrin-dependent firm adhesion and diapedesis.
Endothelial nitric oxide/prostacyclin and endothelin set opposing vascular-tone signals.
Medial smooth muscle is synthetic as well as contractile, producing elastic and reticular fibers and proteoglycans.
Vasa vasorum supply outer wall regions too distant from luminal diffusion; the internal elastic lamina is fenestrated to facilitate diffusion.
examTraps: tPA loss impairs fibrin removal rather than initial platelet adhesion to exposed collagen.
Vasa vasorum do not normally replace luminal nutrition of the intima.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Give the ordered stages of neutrophil exit through a postcapillary venule.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Selectin-mediated rolling, integrin-mediated firm adhesion, diapedesis through opened junctions, then chemotaxis through tissue.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can a large vein have more vasa vasorum than a similarly thick artery?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its luminal blood is less oxygenated, so diffusion supplies less oxygen to the wall.

objectives.text: Predict transport, inflammatory, hemostatic, vasomotor, and nutritive consequences from endothelial and wall specializations.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Elastic and muscular arteries, arterioles, and vascular sensors
concepts.summary: Elastic arteries use many fenestrated elastic lamellae to store systolic energy and sustain diastolic flow; their numerous lamellae make a separate internal elastic lamina difficult to distinguish. Muscular arteries distribute blood with a smooth-muscle-rich media and prominent elastic laminae. Arterioles, with only one to two medial smooth-muscle layers, are the principal resistance vessels controlling capillary-bed inflow. Arteriovenous shunts can bypass capillaries. The carotid sinus is a stretch-sensitive baroreceptor with a thin media and nerve-rich adventitia, whereas the nearby carotid body is a fenestrated-capillary-rich chemoreceptor.
keyPoints: Elastic recoil smooths pulsatile ventricular output and maintains forward flow during diastole.
Muscular arteries have a conspicuous internal elastic lamina and may have an external elastic lamina.
Arteriolar radius is a high-leverage determinant of resistance and downstream capillary pressure.
Carotid sinus and carotid body differ in stimulus, structure, and response.
Portal systems place two capillary beds in series; arteriovenous shunts route blood around capillary beds.
examTraps: A carotid sinus is not a chemoreceptor nodule; that is the carotid body.
A prominent isolated internal elastic lamina favors a muscular artery, not a large elastic artery filled with many lamellae.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the Windkessel role of elastic arteries?
retrievalPrompts.answer: They expand during systole, store energy in elastic lamellae, and recoil during diastole to maintain flow.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do carotid sinus and carotid body differ?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The sinus is a baroreceptive dilation with a thin media and rich innervation; the body is a chemoreceptive cell cluster with many fenestrated capillaries.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Capillary classes, pericytes, and exchange routes
concepts.summary: Capillary exchange depends on endothelial continuity and basal-lamina organization. Continuous capillaries use intercellular junctions plus vesicular transfer and are least permeable in the CNS. Fenestrated capillaries accelerate exchange while retaining a continuous basal lamina; renal glomerular fenestrae uniquely lack diaphragms. Sinusoids have large endothelial gaps and a discontinuous basal lamina for macromolecule and cell passage. Pericytes share the basal lamina, stabilize capillaries and postcapillary venules, can contract, and contribute to repair. Postcapillary venules are the major site of inflammatory extravasation and edema.
keyPoints: Continuous capillaries preserve an uninterrupted endothelial sheet and basal lamina.
Fenestrated capillaries combine endothelial pores with a continuous basal lamina; most pores have diaphragms except in renal glomeruli.
Sinusoids combine discontinuous endothelium and basal lamina to permit very large exchanges.
Pericyte processes surround endothelium within the shared basal lamina and provide contractile, stabilizing, and progenitor-like functions.
Starling forces govern bulk fluid movement; lymphatics normally return the small net filtrate.
examTraps: Do not call a fenestrated capillary a sinusoid when its basal lamina is continuous.
A pericyte is abluminal and basal-lamina-associated, not a second endothelial layer exposed to blood.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Rank continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoidal capillaries by structural permeability.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Continuous are least open, fenestrated add transcellular pores while keeping a continuous basal lamina, and sinusoids have endothelial gaps plus discontinuous basal lamina.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why are postcapillary venules central to inflammation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Their endothelium is specialized for leukocyte adhesion/diapedesis and becomes highly permeable to fluid during inflammatory signaling.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Venous return and lymphatic microanatomy
concepts.summary: Veins are high-capacitance vessels with larger, more irregular lumina and thinner walls than companion arteries. Medium veins often have valves formed by paired intimal folds, and large veins may contain longitudinal smooth muscle in a dominant adventitia. Lymphatic capillaries begin blindly, lack pericytes and a continuous basal lamina, and have overlapping endothelial flaps tethered by anchoring filaments; rising interstitial pressure opens these microvalves. Collecting lymphatics add smooth muscle and valves, while the thoracic duct approaches a vein-like wall.
keyPoints: Venous valves are intimal folds and become more important where return works against gravity.
Large veins have a thin media and thick adventitia that may contain longitudinal smooth muscle.
Initial lymphatics open when interstitial pressure pulls anchoring filaments and separates endothelial overlaps.
The discontinuous or absent basal lamina of initial lymphatics facilitates uptake of protein-rich interstitial fluid.
examTraps: A collapsed, thin-walled profile without erythrocytes may be lymphatic rather than a small vein.
Do not assign pericytes to initial lymphatic capillaries.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What opens an initial lymphatic microvalve?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Increased interstitial pressure pulls anchoring filaments and separates overlapping endothelial flaps.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which tunic dominates a large vein?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The adventitia, often with longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles, dominates over the thin media.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Thymic microenvironments and selection
concepts.summary: The thymus is a lobulated primary lymphoid organ whose epithelial-reticular stroma, rather than reticular fibers, creates cortex and medulla. Dense cortical thymocytes undergo positive selection, then surviving cells move medullaryward for negative selection against self antigens. Cortical epithelial-reticular cells and continuous capillaries help form the blood-thymus barrier. Medullary type VI epithelial-reticular cells form Hassall corpuscles. The organ has no lymphoid nodules and no afferent lymphatics; age-related involution replaces parenchyma with adipose tissue but does not erase all function.
keyPoints: Epithelial-reticular cells form a cytokeratin-positive cellular network linked by desmosomes.
Positive selection is cortical; negative selection is concentrated in the medulla.
The blood-thymus barrier protects developing cortical thymocytes from circulating antigens.
Hassall corpuscles are concentrically arranged type VI epithelial-reticular cells in the medulla.
Thymus lacks lymphoid follicles/nodules and afferent lymphatics.
examTraps: Hassall corpuscles are not germinal centers and do not identify B-cell follicles.
The thymic stroma is epithelial-reticular, not the reticular-fiber framework typical of most secondary lymphoid organs.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where do positive and negative thymocyte selection occur?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Positive selection occurs in cortex; negative selection occurs mainly in medulla.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name two features that distinguish thymus from a lymph node.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Thymus has epithelial-reticular stroma and Hassall corpuscles and lacks lymphoid nodules and afferent lymphatics.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: MALT, lymph-node, and splenic architecture
concepts.summary: Secondary lymphoid organs route antigens through distinct compartments. MALT samples mucosal luminal antigen; intestinal M cells transcytose material to immune cells, and plasma cells support secretory IgA. Lymph nodes filter lymph through subcapsular, trabecular, and medullary sinuses; B-cell follicles occupy cortex, T cells and high endothelial venules occupy paracortex, and medullary cords contain plasma cells. The spleen filters blood: PALS surrounds central arterioles, marginal zones intercept blood-borne antigen, and open circulation sends blood through red-pulp cords before it re-enters stave-cell-lined sinusoids through slits.
keyPoints: M cells transcytose luminal antigen rather than relying on a classic mucociliary barrier.
Lymph-node paracortex is T-cell rich and contains high endothelial venules for lymphocyte entry from blood.
Medullary cords contain plasma cells; sinuses conduct lymph toward efferent vessels.
Splenic PALS is the T-cell compartment around central arterioles; adjacent nodules are B-cell territories.
Open splenic circulation exposes erythrocytes to macrophages in cords before passage through sinusoidal slits.
examTraps: Do not reverse afferent and efferent lymph-node routes.
A central arteriole in white pulp is surrounded by PALS, not a medullary cord.
Splenic sinusoids have elongated stave cells and a discontinuous basal lamina, not high endothelial venules.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace lymph through a lymph node.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Afferent lymphatics enter the subcapsular sinus, then trabecular/cortical sinuses, medullary sinuses, and finally the efferent lymphatic at the hilum.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does open splenic circulation test erythrocyte deformability?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Blood enters red-pulp cords, and erythrocytes must squeeze through narrow slits between stave cells to regain the sinusoidal lumen.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Cardiac induction and heart-field patterning
concepts.summary: Cardiac progenitors enter visceral lateral plate mesoderm and form primary and secondary heart fields. BMP2/4 combined with local WNT inhibition induces NKX2.5. Retinoic acid helps specify caudal venous identity, HAND1/HAND2 support ventricular sidedness, and SHH plus NOTCH-JAG1-FGF signaling expands the secondary field and coordinates cardiac neural crest. Hemodynamic forces then influence which cardiac and arch channels persist.
keyPoints: Primary-heart-field cells supply the entire left ventricle and parts of both atria; secondary-heart-field cells lengthen arterial and venous poles and supply right ventricle, outflow tract, and additional atrial tissue.
Cardiac induction requires permissive BMP signaling and inhibition of WNT3a/8 near anterior cardiogenic mesoderm.
Right and left secondary-heart-field cells make crossed contributions to the outflow region, helping establish the spiral great-artery relationship.
SHH promotes secondary-field proliferation; NOTCH-JAG1-dependent FGF signals regulate neural crest migration and differentiation.
examTraps: BMP alone is insufficient when inhibitory WNT activity persists.
Do not assign the whole heart to one heart field or the entire coronary vasculature to the aorta.
Fine molecular pathways are book extension unless explicitly stated in the lecture transcript.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What two signaling conditions induce NKX2.5 in cardiogenic mesoderm?
retrievalPrompts.answer: BMP2/4 activity together with local inhibition of WNT3a/8 by anterior endodermal inhibitors such as CRESCENT and CERBERUS.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can an SHH defect produce an outflow malalignment?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Reduced SHH-patched signaling lowers secondary-heart-field proliferation, shortens the outflow tract, and impairs later alignment and septation.

objectives.text: Predict cardiac regional and lineage effects of perturbing heart-field induction or laterality.
Relate folding, cardiac jelly, proepicardium, and blood flow to construction of the early heart.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Cardiac looping and segment identities
concepts.summary: Between days 23 and 28, the cephalic tube bends ventrally, caudally, and rightward while the atrial pole moves dorsocranially and leftward. Trabeculation identifies the primitive left ventricle and the proximal bulbar primitive right ventricle. The conus forms both smooth ventricular outflows and the truncus forms the roots and proximal great arteries.
keyPoints: Looping establishes atria posterior to ventricles and moves the conotruncal region toward the midline.
The proximal bulbus forms trabeculated right ventricle, the conus forms both ventricular outflow tracts, and truncus forms the roots and proximal aorta and pulmonary artery.
Leftward rather than rightward looping produces dextrocardia and can occur without complete situs inversus.
During normal D-looping, the bulbus cordis moves ventrally, caudally, and rightward while the atrial region shifts dorsally, cranially, and leftward.
examTraps: Do not call the entire bulbus cordis an outflow tract.
Dextrocardia can reflect a local looping error or an earlier laterality disorder; the stem must distinguish them.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the opposing vectors during normal cardiac looping?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The cephalic portion moves ventral, caudal, and right; the atrial portion moves dorsal, cranial, and left.

objectives.text: Apply looping vectors and heart-tube segment derivatives to developmental lesions.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Sinus venosus and pulmonary-vein incorporation
concepts.summary: Left-to-right venous shunts enlarge the right sinus horn and shift the sinuatrial orifice rightward. The right horn becomes sinus venarum, while left-horn remnants form coronary sinus and oblique left-atrial vein. The dorsal mesenchymal protrusion positions a separately developing pulmonary vein in the left atrium, whose expansion incorporates the stem to create four ostia.
keyPoints: Each early sinus horn receives vitelline, umbilical, and common cardinal veins.
Inferior right venous-valve tissue forms the valves of the IVC and coronary sinus; crista terminalis marks the incorporated right-horn boundary.
The pulmonary vein forms within the dorsal mesenchymal protrusion and is not simply an atrial endothelial outgrowth in the modern account.
Rightward displacement of the dorsal mesenchymal protrusion provides a mechanism for TAPVR and its association with heterotaxy.
examTraps: Do not reverse left- and right-sinus-horn derivatives.
A probe-patent foramen ovale is an oblique flap cleft and need not produce chronic shunting.
The lecture transcript is ambiguous about pulmonary-vein growth direction; the book account controls.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What creates the four pulmonary-vein ostia?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Left-atrial expansion incorporates the single main pulmonary-vein stem up to its four branch points.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does the crista terminalis separate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Primitive trabeculated right atrium from smooth sinus venarum derived from the right sinus horn.

objectives.text: Trace sinus-horn, venous-valve, and pulmonary-vein remodeling into adult atrial anatomy.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Endocardial cushions, atrial septation, and AV canals
concepts.summary: Cardiac jelly expands into endocardial cushions whose cellular sources differ by region: endocardium supplies AV cushions, while cardiac neural crest populates conotruncal cushions. Atrial septation preserves flow by opening ostium secundum before ostium primum closes. Dorsal and ventral AV cushions divide the common canal and contribute to the atrial and membranous ventricular septal cross.
keyPoints: Endocardial-cushion morphogenesis requires extracellular-matrix deposition, cell migration, and proliferation.
Septum primum closes ostium primum against the cushions while apoptosis creates ostium secundum.
Septum secundum overlaps the secundum opening; residual septum primum forms its valve.
Rightward AV-canal expansion gives the common atrium access to both primitive ventricles before canal division.
examTraps: Ostium secundum is an apoptosis-created opening in septum primum; foramen ovale is the opening left by incomplete septum secundum.
Functional closure at birth depends on an atrial pressure reversal, not immediate anatomical fusion.
Persistent common AV canal has both atrial and ventricular components, unlike an isolated secundum defect.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why must ostium secundum form before ostium primum closes?
retrievalPrompts.answer: To preserve continuous fetal right-to-left interatrial flow while the lower opening is sealed.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which cells populate AV versus conotruncal cushions?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Endocardial cells populate AV cushions; migrating cardiac neural crest populates conotruncal cushions.

objectives.text: Predict septal consequences of altered cushion lineage, matrix, apoptosis, or AV-canal alignment.
Trace cushion-derived AV leaflets and their supporting apparatus.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: AV valves, ventricular septum, and conotruncal outflow
concepts.summary: AV leaflets are hollowed from cushion-derived mesenchyme and retain muscular cords that become connective-tissue chordae attached to papillary muscles. Truncal cushions spiral into the aorticopulmonary septum, conal cushions assign ventricular outflows, and cushion plus conus tissue closes the interventricular foramen above the muscular septum. Semilunar cusps form by hollowing three tubercles in each channel.
keyPoints: Conus septation gives an anterolateral right-ventricular outflow and posteromedial left-ventricular outflow.
The membranous interventricular septum requires contact among AV-cushion, conus-septum, and muscular-septum components.
Semilunar cusps lack chordae and form by excavation of truncal tubercles.
Tricuspid atresia requires alternate atrial and ventricular communications; Ebstein anomaly displaces leaflets apically.
examTraps: AV and semilunar valves use different morphogenetic mechanisms.
Do not attribute muscular VSD and membranous VSD to the same failed fusion.
Right-ventricular hypertrophy in tetralogy is a secondary pressure response, not one of the direct partitioning events.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What closes the embryonic interventricular foramen?
retrievalPrompts.answer: AV-cushion tissue extends over the muscular septum and fuses with adjacent conus-septum components.

objectives.text: Apply AV-valve, conus, truncus, semilunar, and ventricular-septum mechanisms.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Congenital cardiac mechanism patterns
concepts.summary: Congenital cardiac patterns become interpretable when each anatomy is tied to a failed developmental process. Laterality errors can invert ventricles, excessive septum-primum resorption or deficient septum secundum can create secundum ASDs, conotruncal displacement produces tetralogy, absent ridges produce persistent truncus with VSD, and a straight septum produces transposition. Ductal patency becomes life-sustaining in selected outflow atresias.
keyPoints: Tetralogy follows anterior conotruncal displacement; right-ventricular hypertrophy is secondary to obstruction.
Persistent truncus is obligatorily linked to VSD because ridge tissue also helps close the interventricular foramen.
Aortic atresia and pulmonary atresia require opposite directions of ductal flow to supply the obstructed circuit.
22q11 deletion links craniofacial and pharyngeal abnormalities with conotruncal defects through neural crest.
examTraps: Transposition has two separate trunks connected to the wrong ventricles; persistent truncus has one undivided trunk.
Ventricular inversion concerns morphologic ventricular identity and laterality, not simply straight conotruncal septation.
Ectopia cordis is a ventral body-wall closure defect.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does persistent truncus include a VSD?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The missing conotruncal ridge tissue normally partitions the outflow and participates with AV-cushion tissue in membranous septal closure.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the direction of ductal flow in pulmonary atresia?
retrievalPrompts.answer: From aorta to pulmonary artery, opposite the predominant fetal direction.

objectives.text: Infer a developmental lesion from a congenital cardiac anatomy and its required compensatory flow.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Myocardial origin of the conduction system
concepts.summary: Pacemaker activity begins broadly in myocardium, localizes to the caudal left tube, transfers to sinus venosus, and becomes the SAN near the SVC after incorporation. AV-canal cells coalesce into the AV node. The intrinsic nodes, bundles, branches, and Purkinje fibers are primary cardiac-myocyte derivatives; autonomic fibers regulate rather than construct them. TBX3 preserves conduction fate by suppressing ventricular-muscle differentiation.
keyPoints: SAN location reflects incorporation of sinus-venosus pacemaker tissue.
AVN location reflects coalescence of specialized cells around the AV canal.
TBX3 blocks working-myocardial differentiation in conduction precursors.
All early myocardial cells can act as pacemakers; dominant pacemaker activity localizes during development, and the heart begins beating at approximately day 21.
examTraps: The intrinsic conduction system is not a neural crest derivative.
Autonomic innervation changes rate but does not generate the SAN lineage.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does TBX3 do in conduction precursors?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It inhibits ventricular-muscle differentiation, permitting specialized conduction-system identity.

objectives.text: Trace conduction tissues to their myocardial sources and developmental positions.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Aortic arches and definitive arteries
concepts.summary: Major channels begin by vasculogenesis and expand by angiogenesis. Aortic arches appear sequentially, remodel asymmetrically under flow, laterality, ectodermal and endodermal signals, and neural crest. Adult vessels are composites: aortic-sac horns, arches, dorsal aortae, and seventh intersegmental arteries each contribute defined segments. Abnormal persistence or regression produces aberrant subclavian vessels, vascular rings, and interrupted arches.
keyPoints: Five numbered arch pairs occur because the fifth is absent or incomplete and the others are not all present simultaneously.
The right subclavian combines right fourth arch, right dorsal aorta, and right seventh intersegmental artery.
Normal regression removes the carotid duct and distal right dorsal aorta.
Epicardial-derived coronary endothelial cells connect to the aorta by ingrowth rather than aortic outgrowth.
examTraps: The aortic arch between left common carotid and left subclavian is left fourth arch; the more proximal segment is left aortic-sac horn.
Aberrant right subclavian is usually a retroesophageal single vessel; double arch is a complete vascular ring.
Type B interrupted arch lies between left common carotid and left subclavian and is linked to 22q11 deletion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What three embryonic components form the right subclavian artery?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Right fourth arch proximally, right dorsal aorta in the middle, and right seventh intersegmental artery distally.

objectives.text: Assemble definitive arterial segments and predict anomalies from persistence or regression.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Vitelline, umbilical, and cardinal venous remodeling
concepts.summary: The liver interrupts vitelline veins to create hepatic sinusoids and a dominant right hepatocardiac channel. The surviving left umbilical vein connects to it through ductus venosus. Cardinal, subcardinal, sacrocardinal, and supracardinal systems then assemble the SVC, IVC, brachiocephalic, renal, gonadal, azygos, and hemiazygos veins. Anomalies reflect persistence or loss of normally asymmetric channels.
keyPoints: The hepatic IVC is right vitelline, renal IVC is right subcardinal, and caudal IVC is right sacrocardinal.
Anterior-cardinal anastomosis forms the left brachiocephalic vein; right common plus proximal right anterior cardinal forms SVC.
Subcardinal anastomosis forms left renal vein; distal left subcardinal persists as left gonadal vein.
Supracardinal veins take over body-wall drainage and form azygos and hemiazygos channels.
examTraps: Left SVC and double SVC are not identical: the latter retains both sides and lacks the normal communicating brachiocephalic vein.
Absent IVC may drain caudal blood through azygos continuation while hepatic veins still enter the right atrium.
The vessel-2 transcript contains an unreliable ASR phrase near hepatic IVC; Langman assigns it to the right vitelline hepatocardiac channel.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the three-segment origin of the IVC?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Right vitelline hepatocardiac, right subcardinal, and right sacrocardinal channels from cranial to caudal.

objectives.text: Derive adult systemic veins and anomalies from embryonic venous channels.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Fetal streaming and circulatory transition
concepts.summary: Placental blood uses ductus venosus to approach the IVC, whose valve directs the better-oxygenated stream across the foramen ovale. SVC blood preferentially enters the right ventricle and bypasses high-resistance lungs through ductus arteriosus. At birth, placental separation lowers right-atrial pressure and lung expansion raises left-atrial pressure. Muscular contraction closes fetal vessels functionally before slower anatomical obliteration.
keyPoints: A ductus-venosus sphincter buffers excessive placental return during uterine contractions.
Preferential streaming sends better-oxygenated blood to coronary and carotid arteries before ductal mixing in descending aorta.
Bradykinin released with lung inflation contracts ductus arteriosus; intimal proliferation completes closure over one to three months.
Foramen-ovale closure is initially reversible and may take about a year to fuse anatomically.
examTraps: The umbilical vein is oxygenated and returns from placenta; umbilical arteries return lower-saturation blood to placenta.
Ductus arteriosus normally carries pulmonary-trunk blood into descending aorta, whereas ductus venosus is a hepatic venous bypass.
Crying can transiently reopen a functionally closed atrial flap before fusion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why do brain and myocardium receive the best-oxygenated fetal stream?
retrievalPrompts.answer: IVC blood is directed across the foramen ovale to the left heart, and coronary and carotid arteries branch early from the ascending aorta.

objectives.text: Trace preferential fetal flow and explain functional and anatomical closure at birth.

concepts.title: Intracardiac landmarks and coronary routes
concepts.summary: Intracardiac anatomy is most useful when landmarks are treated as connected routes rather than isolated labels. The atrial and ventricular partitions locate conduction tissue, valve-related outflow tracts organize flow, and coronary arterial and venous paths explain what is endangered by a focal intervention.
keyPoints: The triangle of Koch localizes the atrioventricular node; the penetrating atrioventricular bundle is the normal electrical bridge across the insulating atrioventricular junction.
The supraventricular crest separates right-ventricular inflow from the infundibular outlet, whereas the aortic vestibule is the smooth left-ventricular outflow region.
The floor of the fossa ovalis is valve-derived chiefly from septum primum; the adult limbus is an atrial-wall infolding and should not be reduced to a simple septum-secundum label.
Anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior right ventricle directly to the right atrium, while smallest cardiac veins drain subendocardial myocardium directly into chambers.
Nodal arterial supply varies: the atrioventricular node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery, and the sinuatrial nodal artery may arise from the circumflex artery.
examTraps: Do not infer a structure from a famous eponym alone; first identify the chamber, wall and direction of flow.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which landmark triangle identifies the atrioventricular node, and what forms its three sides?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The triangle of Koch: tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet and coronary sinus ostium; the AV node lies near its apex.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast anterior cardiac veins with smallest cardiac veins.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Anterior cardiac veins drain anterior right ventricular myocardium directly to the right atrium; smallest cardiac veins drain subendocardial myocardium directly into one or more chambers.

concepts.title: Pericardial access and cardiophrenic relations
concepts.summary: The fibrous pericardium is a spatial organizer for nerves, vessels and safe access routes. Tracing the phrenic nerve on the pericardium and the vagus behind the lung root turns memorized relations into procedural predictions.
keyPoints: The phrenic nerve and pericardiacophrenic vessels descend between fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
A subxiphoid pericardiocentesis route is directed superiorly and posteriorly toward the left shoulder while avoiding pleural entry when properly placed.
The phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung root; the vagus passes posterior to it.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch close to the ligamentum arteriosum, within the aortopulmonary region.
examTraps: The phrenic and vagus relations are to the lung root, not simply to the lung as a whole.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What structures share the plane between fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The phrenic nerve and pericardiacophrenic vessels.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does an aortic-arch lesion cause hoarseness but a pericardial incision threaten diaphragmatic function?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch; the phrenic nerve descends on the fibrous pericardium.

concepts.title: Mediastinal pathways and collateral routes
concepts.summary: Posterior and superior mediastinal anatomy is a network of crossings and alternate routes. Veins cross the arch, the thoracic duct changes side, the azygos system links caval territories, and intercostal channels enlarge when the aorta is narrowed.
keyPoints: The left superior intercostal vein crosses the aortic arch lateral to the left vagus and medial to the left phrenic nerve before reaching the left brachiocephalic vein.
The thoracic duct crosses toward the left near T5; disruption below this crossing tends to produce right chylothorax and above it left chylothorax.
The hemiazygos vein crosses posterior to the aorta and oesophagus around T8-T9 to reach the azygos vein.
Azygos-continuous ascending lumbar channels create collateral communication between inferior and superior caval territories.
Pericardiacophrenic branches arise from internal thoracic arteries, while posterior intercostal arteries enlarge as collaterals around coarctation.
examTraps: A crossing level predicts laterality only after establishing whether the structure is still on the right or has moved to the left.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does thoracic-duct crossing level predict the side of chylothorax?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Below its approximate T5 crossing the duct is predominantly right-sided; above the crossing it is left-sided.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name one venous and one arterial bypass pathway relevant to caval or aortic obstruction.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Azygos-ascending lumbar continuity can bypass caval obstruction; intercostal/internal thoracic-scapular networks can bypass aortic narrowing.

concepts.title: Thoracic wall, breast and axial spaces
concepts.summary: Thoracic wall and breast anatomy becomes clinically predictive when fascial planes, lymphatic continuity and axial boundaries are combined. These relationships explain tumor mobility, contralateral spread, procedural nerve risk and imaging spaces.
keyPoints: Parasternal lymphatic channels can cross the sternum, allowing medial breast disease to reach contralateral nodes.
The retromammary space permits normal mobility of the breast on deep fascia; fixation suggests posterior invasion.
The main intercostal bundle lies in the costal groove, with a smaller collateral bundle near the superior border of the rib below.

The sternal-angle plane separates superior and inferior mediastina and conventionally locates the aortic arch ends and carina. Actual adult carinal height varies and is commonly inferior to this plane; avoid treating a surface landmark as an invariant CT measurement.
The aortopulmonary interval lies between the aortic arch and left pulmonary artery, with trachea medial and left lung lateral.
examTraps: Entering just above a rib avoids the main costal-groove bundle but does not make the collateral bundle disappear.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Integrity of the retromammary plane; posterior invasion reduces mobility.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Electrical events, pump mechanics, and pressure interpretation
concepts.summary: This module links electrical events, pump mechanics, and pressure interpretation to explicit causal reasoning and calculations. Study the source-grounded checkpoints, retrieve the answers without options, then solve the linked original scenarios. Difficulty ratings are editorial, not university-calibrated.
keyPoints: Ventricular phase 0 depends primarily on fast sodium channels; nodal upstrokes and ventricular plateaus depend on calcium entry in different ways.
The ventricular refractory period overlaps most of contraction, preventing the repeated summation that would interfere with ventricular filling.
Stroke volume is end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume. Ejection fraction divides stroke volume by end-diastolic volume, not by end-systolic volume.
Preload, afterload, contractility, and external cardiac pressure are distinct variables; a pressure alone is not proof of a large ventricular filling volume.
Atrial a, c, and v waves reflect atrial contraction, early ventricular systolic AV-valve bulging, and venous filling against a closed AV valve.
examTraps: Name which variable is held fixed before predicting a pressure–volume change; pressure and volume are not interchangeable.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A drug suppresses the rapid ventricular phase-0 upstroke but does not directly inhibit L-type calcium channels. Which comparison with the sinoatrial node is most accurate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Fast sodium-current block directly depresses ventricular phase 0 more than the nodal calcium-dependent upstroke. Working ventricular muscle uses a fast sodium upstroke. Typical SA nodal cells have a calcium-dependent upstroke, so the same sodium-current block does not have an identical direct effect at both sites.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: An isolated ventricle receives a second ordinary stimulus halfway through its first contraction. Why does this fail to produce skeletal-muscle-like summation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Most of the contraction coincides with an action-potential refractory period. The prolonged cardiac action potential and refractory period prevent ordinary repeated excitation during most of contraction. This helps preserve alternating ejection and filling.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Immediately after an isolated rise in aortic pressure, preload and intrinsic contractility are initially unchanged. Which first-beat change is expected?
retrievalPrompts.answer: More blood remains at end systole and stroke volume falls. The ventricle must eject against a greater afterload. At unchanged initial filling and contractility, emptying is reduced: end-systolic volume rises and stroke volume falls. Later reflexes and filling changes are excluded.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Two beats have the same 120-mL end-diastolic volume. End-systolic volume falls from 60 to 40 mL after a positive inotropic stimulus at unchanged afterload. What happens to ejection fraction?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It rises from 50% to approximately 67%. Initially SV = 120 − 60 = 60 mL and EF = 60/120 = 50%. Afterward SV = 80 mL and EF = 80/120 ≈ 67%. Improved emptying is not an increase in preload here.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Atrial fibrillation removes coordinated atrial contraction. Which normal atrial pressure feature is directly lost, rather than simply shifted in timing?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The a wave. The a wave is generated by coordinated atrial contraction. The c wave is linked mainly to AV-valve bulging at ventricular contraction, and the v wave to venous atrial filling during AV-valve closure.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can losing atrial contraction cause more symptoms in a patient with a stiff ventricle than in a healthy resting subject?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A stiff ventricle relies more on the late atrial contribution to filling. Reduced early passive filling makes the atrial booster contribution more important. Losing it can lower ventricular filling and output despite continued ventricular contraction.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Hemodynamic calculations and competing vascular effects
concepts.summary: This module links hemodynamic calculations and competing vascular effects to explicit causal reasoning and calculations. Study the source-grounded checkpoints, retrieve the answers without options, then solve the linked original scenarios. Difficulty ratings are editorial, not university-calibrated.
keyPoints: Flow is driven by inlet minus outlet pressure. Raising both pressures equally does not change flow in a rigid fixed-resistance model.
For ideal laminar tube flow, resistance varies with viscosity and length and inversely with the fourth power of radius; combine simultaneous changes multiplicatively.
Parallel vascular beds share the pressure difference; their conductances add, so blocking one bed increases total resistance of the network.
Reynolds number increases with velocity, diameter, and density and decreases with viscosity. A lower viscosity can increase turbulence tendency even as resistance falls.
Pressure-pulse propagation is not the same as bulk movement of blood. Lower arterial compliance increases pulse pressure for a given stroke volume.

In a classical Starling calculation, hydrostatic and oncotic gradients have opposite signs; lymphatic return is crucial and the simple equation is not a universal steady-state venous-reabsorption rule.
examTraps: Do not copy the reversed turbulence inequalities in Circulatory System 3 slide 14; the textbook states that increasing Reynolds number increases turbulence tendency.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A rigid vessel initially has inlet/outlet pressures of 110/10 mm Hg. Both rise by 20 mm Hg without changing resistance. What happens to flow?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It remains unchanged because the driving pressure difference is still 100 mm Hg. Flow = (Pin − Pout)/R. Both gradients equal 100 mm Hg. This idealized result assumes resistance and vessel geometry remain fixed.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: In an ideal laminar vessel, radius doubles and viscosity also doubles; length and pressure gradient remain fixed. What is the new flow relative to baseline?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Eight times baseline. Q is proportional to r⁴/η. The radius gives a factor of 16 and doubled viscosity divides that by 2: Qnew/Qold = 8.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Two identical vascular beds, each of resistance R, run in parallel. One becomes completely occluded, and perfusion pressure stays constant. What happens to total flow?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It halves because equivalent resistance rises from R/2 to R. Two equal parallel resistances provide twice the conductance of one. Occluding one removes half of that conductance at unchanged pressure.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: At fixed blood velocity, vessel diameter, and density, anemia lowers viscosity. What combined prediction follows from the ideal flow relationships?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Resistance falls while the tendency toward turbulence increases. Viscosity contributes directly to laminar resistance but appears in the denominator of Reynolds number. These are different relationships, so both changes can coexist.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Stroke volume remains 70 mL while effective arterial compliance falls from 2 to 1 mL/mm Hg. Using the simplified SV/compliance estimate, how does pulse pressure change?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It increases from 35 to 70 mm Hg. PP ≈ SV/C gives 70/2 = 35 and 70/1 = 70 mm Hg. Real pulse shape also reflects ejection and wave reflection, so this is a simplified estimate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A pulse is detected rapidly at the wrist after ventricular ejection. What travels from the aorta to the wrist much faster than the average blood itself?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A pressure/distension wave through the arterial system. Pulse-wave velocity describes propagation of a pressure disturbance. It should not be interpreted as the speed of an individual blood cell over the same distance.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: In a stated classical Starling model, Pc = 30, Pi = −2, plasma oncotic pressure = 25, and interstitial oncotic pressure = 3 mm Hg; reflection coefficient = 1. What is the net outward driving pressure?
retrievalPrompts.answer: 10 mm Hg outward. NFP = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi) = (30 − (−2)) − (25 − 3) = 32 − 22 = +10 mm Hg. The question specifies the classical model; it is not asserting permanent reabsorption at every venous capillary end.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Venous drainage from a limb is obstructed while arterial inflow persists. Which immediate change most directly promotes local edema?
retrievalPrompts.answer: An increase in upstream capillary hydrostatic pressure. Impaired venous outflow raises capillary-side hydrostatic pressure and favors filtration. Lymphatic reserve can initially compensate but may be exceeded.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Cardiac output, venous return, and coronary supply–demand
concepts.summary: This module links cardiac output, venous return, and coronary supply–demand to explicit causal reasoning and calculations. Study the source-grounded checkpoints, retrieve the answers without options, then solve the linked original scenarios. Difficulty ratings are editorial, not university-calibrated.
keyPoints: Fick cardiac output divides oxygen consumption by the arterial–mixed-venous oxygen content difference; convert per-deciliter content to per-liter before calculating liters per minute.
In the simple venous-return model, flow depends on mean systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure, divided by resistance to venous return.
A high right atrial pressure is not proof of good output; impaired pumping or external cardiac compression can raise pressure while reducing forward flow.
Coronary oxygen delivery must meet demand. Tachycardia shortens diastolic supply time, while sympathetic stimulation raises myocardial work and oxygen use.
Direct sympathetic vascular actions and indirect metabolic coronary vasodilation must be distinguished; net flow in an active heart follows metabolic demand.
examTraps: These detailed Fick/venous-return applications extend the lecture-level pump and circulation material; they are labeled book extension, not confirmed faculty questions.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: At steady state, oxygen consumption is 300 mL/min, arterial oxygen content 20 mL/dL, and mixed-venous content 14 mL/dL. What is cardiac output?
retrievalPrompts.answer: 5 L/min. The content difference is 6 mL/dL = 60 mL/L. CO = 300/60 = 5 L/min. Use oxygen content, not a difference in oxygen partial pressures.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Mean systemic filling pressure is 9 mm Hg and resistance to venous return is 2 mm Hg/(L/min). If right atrial pressure rises from 1 to 5 mm Hg with the other values fixed, how does venous return change?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It falls from 4 to 2 L/min. VR = (Pms − Pra)/Rvr. Initially (9−1)/2 = 4; afterward (9−5)/2 = 2 L/min. Raising downstream right atrial pressure opposes return in this isolated model.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A patient has elevated measured right atrial pressure, reduced ventricular filling, and low output caused by pericardial compression. Which interpretation is best?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Elevated intracavitary pressure does not ensure adequate transmural distending pressure. External pressure can elevate the pressure measured inside the heart while limiting chamber distension. Distending pressure depends on inside minus surrounding pressure, not the intracavitary reading alone.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Marked tachycardia worsens left-ventricular ischemia despite a higher heart rate. Which paired mechanism best explains this?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Less diastolic coronary perfusion time together with greater myocardial oxygen demand. Left-ventricular intramural vessels are compressed during systole, so much perfusion occurs in diastole. Faster rates shorten diastole disproportionately while increasing work and oxygen demand.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: During sympathetic cardiac stimulation, coronary flow rises even though some coronary vessels have constrictor alpha receptors. Why is this not a contradiction?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Increased myocardial metabolism produces local vasodilation that can outweigh direct vasoconstriction. Separate the direct neural action on vessels from the indirect response to increased heart rate and contractile work. The active myocardium requires more oxygen and generates local vasodilator signals.
